passages.title: The Tall Tower
sentences: Sam, Ana and Ben played a block game at a table.
They stacked blocks to make a tower.
The tower got very tall.
Then Pixel ran under the table to get his ball.
His tail hit a table leg, and the table shook.
The tower fell down.
Everyone laughed.
Then they started a new game.

passages.title: Rain on Match Day
sentences: On Saturday, Ana had a soccer match.
She put on her red shirt and her soccer shoes.
Then it started to rain very hard.
The field got wet and muddy.
The coach moved the match to next Saturday.
Ana frowned and sat down.
Then she played a soccer video game with Ben at home.

passages.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
sentences: It was a hot, dry day, and a crow was very thirsty.
She flew down to a tall pitcher of water.
The water was low, at the very bottom of the pitcher.
Her beak was too short to reach it.
The crow looked around and saw some small stones.
She picked up one stone and dropped it into the pitcher.
The water rose a little bit.
She dropped in more stones, one by one.
Each stone pushed the water higher.
Finally, the water was near the top, and the crow drank it.

credit.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Priya's Rover Stops
sentences: On Thursday, Priya took her rover to the park to test it on the grass.
She drove it in a big circle around a bench.
Then the rover slowed down and stopped in the middle of the path.
The little light on top had turned red.
Priya remembered that a red light means the battery is empty.
She had played with the rover all morning and forgot to charge it.
Priya carried the rover home and plugged it in.
After one hour, the light turned green, and the rover worked again.

passages.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
sentences: A hare liked to tell everyone that he was the fastest animal in the forest.
One day, a tortoise said, "Let's have a race."
The hare laughed, because he was sure he would win.
The animals marked a path from the big oak tree to the river.
When the race began, the hare ran so fast that he was soon far ahead.
He looked back and saw that the tortoise was far behind him.
"I have lots of time," thought the hare, so he lay down under a tree for a nap.
The hare fell asleep, and he slept for a long time.
Meanwhile, the tortoise walked slowly and steadily, one step at a time.
He passed the sleeping hare and kept going.
When the hare woke up, he ran as fast as he could.
But the tortoise had already crossed the finish line by the river.

credit.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Domino Run
sentences: On Friday after school, Leo and Maya built a domino run in the school library.
It had five hundred dominoes and went around two tables.
Mr. Hill said they could start it at four o'clock so the club could watch.
Ten minutes before four o'clock, a strong wind blew in through an open window.
It pushed a sheet of paper off a desk, and the paper slid into the last domino.
That domino hit the next one, and a long line fell backward.
Maya gasped, and Leo ran to the middle of the line.
He pulled out three dominoes to make a gap, and the line stopped falling at the gap.
Only fifty had fallen.
Maya closed the window, and they set the fallen ones up again.
At four o'clock, the club watched the whole run fall in a perfect line.

passages.title: Leo's Wet Socks
sentences: Leo skated home from the park.
Dark gray clouds filled the sky.
Soon, the streets were wet, and there were puddles everywhere.
Leo got home and took off his shoes.
His socks were very wet.
He put them by the heater to dry.

passages.title: The Empty Plate
sentences: Grandma Rose put a plate of ham sandwiches on the low table in the living room.
Then she went to the kitchen to make some tea.
Sam was upstairs, building a model train track.
Pixel stayed in the living room, next to the sandwiches.
Five minutes later, Grandma Rose came back with the tea.
The plate was empty, and there were crumbs on the rug.
Pixel was licking his nose and wagging his tail.
Sam was still upstairs with his train track.

passages.title: The Bird Bowl
sentences: On Friday evening, Ben filled a bowl with water for the birds.
He put it on the back step.
That night, the weather report said it would be very cold.
In the morning, Ben went out to check the bowl.
The water was hard and cold, and it stayed in the bowl when he tipped it.
A small bird landed on top of it and slid across.
Ben smiled and went inside to get some warm water.

passages.title: The Snapped Chain
sentences: On Saturday morning, Leo and Ben rode their bikes to the trails in Story Woods.
They planned to ride up to the old mill and eat lunch by the creek.
Halfway up the first hill, Ben's chain snapped with a loud click.
His pedals spun around, but the back wheel did not move.
Ben got off and looked at the broken chain lying in the dirt.
"Okay, let's think about what we can do," Leo said in a calm voice.
They could push both bikes up to the mill, but that was two more miles.
They could call Ben's dad, but he was at work until three o'clock.
Or they could walk back down to Okafor's Bike Shop, which was only ten minutes away.
They chose the bike shop.
Mr. Okafor fixed the chain with a new link while the boys waited.
Then they rode back up the hill and ate a late lunch by the creek.

passages.title: No Ferry Today
sentences: For three weeks, Ms. Ortiz's science class had been getting ready for a trip to Seal Point.
Seal Point is a rocky island across the bay, where dozens of seals rest in the sun.
The plan was to take the nine o'clock ferry, count the seals and record what each one was doing.
Sam had even drawn a map of the island that showed the best places to stand.
But on Tuesday morning, a strong wind was pushing tall, gray waves into the harbor.
When the class reached the dock, a sign on the ferry office said, "All ferries cancelled today because of high wind."
A few students groaned, and Sam slowly folded his map in half.
Ms. Ortiz read the sign twice, and then she turned to face the class.
"Our plan has changed, so let's look at our choices," she said in a calm voice.
She wrote three choices in her notebook and read them aloud.
The class could go back to school and watch a video about seals.
They could wait on the dock in case the wind dropped.
Or they could visit the Sea Center next to the ferry office, which has a touch tank full of crabs and sea stars.
Priya pointed to the word "today" on the sign and asked Ms. Ortiz to cross out waiting.
Ben said a video would be fine, but at the Sea Center they could study real animals.
The class voted, and most students chose the Sea Center.
Inside, they counted eleven crabs and seven sea stars, and Sam drew a new map that showed where each animal was hiding.
Before they walked back to school, Ms. Ortiz phoned the ferry company and moved the Seal Point trip to the next Tuesday.

passages.title: The Dough That Did Not Rise
sentences: Every Saturday, Rose's Bakery sells forty loaves of seed bread, and Sam helps Grandma Rose bake them.
On Friday evening, she mixes the dough and leaves it in big bowls so it can rise slowly overnight.
Dough rises because yeast, a tiny living thing in the dough, makes bubbles of gas when it is warm.
But this Saturday, when Sam lifted the towels off the bowls, the dough was just as flat as it had been the night before.
Grandma Rose did not panic.
"Let's check one thing at a time," she said.
First, Sam read the recipe card while Grandma Rose checked her notes from the night before, and every amount matched.
Next, they looked at the yeast packet, and its date showed that it was still fresh.
Then Sam noticed that his fingers felt cold, so he looked at the thermometer on the wall.
It showed only 48 degrees, which was much colder than the bakery usually was.
Grandma Rose checked the heater and found that it had switched off.
A storm had made the power go out for a short time in the night, and the heater had not turned back on.
Grandma Rose nodded, because now she knew why the dough was still flat.
She pressed the heater's reset button, and warm air began to blow.
Then she and Sam moved the bowls beside the warm oven and covered them with clean towels.
Sam made a sign for the door that said, "Fresh bread at 11 AM today. Thank you for waiting!"
By ten o'clock, the dough had doubled in size, and at eleven the first warm loaves were on the shelves.

credit.title: The Dough That Did Not Rise
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: The Rained-Out Final
sentences: Ana and Ben's soccer team had won every game that autumn, and the league final was set for Saturday morning at the Harbor Middle School field.
Grandma Rose had promised to bring orange slices, and Sam had painted a banner for the fence.
But on Friday night, heavy rain began to fall, and it was still falling the next morning.
When the twins reached the field in their raincoats, wide puddles covered the center circle, and the grass squelched under their shoes.
Their coach was already there, talking with the groundskeeper, who looks after the school's grass.
A few minutes later, she told the team that the league did not allow games on a flooded field, so the final could not be played that day.
Ben stared at the puddles and let out a long breath, but he did not argue.
"We have a problem to solve," the coach said, "so let's look at every choice before we pick one."
Grandma Rose offered the back room of her bakery, just across the street, as a dry place to think.
There, the coach wrote four choices on a large sheet of paper.
The team could play in the school gym that afternoon, play on the field on Sunday, play on the following Saturday, or share the trophy with the other team without playing.
Next, they checked each choice carefully.
Ana phoned the school office and learned that a basketball tournament had booked the gym for the entire weekend.
Ben opened the weather map on his tablet, which showed rain until late Saturday night and then sunshine all day on Sunday.
However, the groundskeeper had explained that soaked grass needs two full dry days before it is firm enough for a game.
Sharing the trophy was still possible, but nobody on the team wanted to finish the season without playing the final.
Only one choice was left: the following Saturday.
Before anyone cheered, the coach phoned the other team's coach to make sure the new date worked for both teams, and he agreed.
The team spent the rest of the morning in the bakery, planning new plays and eating Grandma Rose's orange slices.
One week later, the final was played under a clear sky on a dry, firm field.

passages.title: The Upside-Down Map
sentences: Sam and Ben wanted to hike to the old mill in Story Woods.
Sam carried the trail map, and Pixel walked next to him.
At a fork in the trail, Sam looked at the map and turned left.
Twenty minutes later, the boys came to the creek, not the mill.
Sam looked at the map again.
The arrow for north was pointing down at his shoes.
He had held the map upside down, so he had turned the wrong way.
Sam turned the map the right way up.
Then the boys walked back to the fork and turned right.
Soon they saw the old mill in front of them.

passages.title: Clouds over Lantern Peaks
sentences: On Friday night, Sam, Maya and Grandma Rose drove up to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
They wanted to watch a meteor shower.
Meteors are tiny bits of space dust and rock that burn up high in the sky and make bright streaks of light.
But when they got out of the car, thick clouds covered the whole sky.
They could not see a single star.
Maya sighed, and Sam stared up at the gray sky.
Then Grandma Rose said, "Our plan has changed, so let's think about what we can do."
They could wait in the car and hope the clouds would move.
They could drive home right away.
Or they could visit the observatory next to the lookout, which was open late.
They chose the observatory.
Inside, a guide showed them photos of meteors and said the shower would go on for three more nights.
Sam checked the weather report, and it said the sky would be clear on Saturday.
So on Saturday night, they drove back up and counted twenty-two meteors.

passages.title: The Silent Keyboard
sentences: Ben plays the keyboard in the Harbor Middle School band.
On Monday night, he practiced a new song at home.
He wore headphones, so the music would not bother Ana while she did her homework.
When he finished, he packed the keyboard into its case.
He did not unplug the headphones, so they went into the case too.
The next day, the band met in the music room to practice.
Ben switched on his keyboard, and the green power light came on.
But when he pressed the keys, the speakers made no sound at all.
Leo, who plays the drums, came over to help.
Leo saw a thin black cord going from the back of the keyboard into the case.
It led to Ben's headphones.
On his keyboard, when headphones are plugged in, the sound goes only to them and not to the speakers.
Ben unplugged the headphones and pressed a key, and a clear note rang out.
The band started the new song on time.

passages.title: The Dull Agates
sentences: For a month, Maya had been polishing beach agates in a rock tumbler in Ms. Ortiz's classroom.
A rock tumbler is a small barrel that turns slowly, day and night, with stones, water and grit inside.
Grit is a sandy powder that grinds the stones smooth.
Every week, Maya washed the stones and the barrel, and then she added a finer grit.
In the last week, she used a polish that should make the agates bright and shiny.
But when Maya opened the barrel on Friday, the agates were dull and cloudy.
Under a magnifying glass, she could see tiny scratches all over them.
Ms. Ortiz explained that scratches like these usually come from coarse grit, the roughest kind, which Maya had used in the first week.
Together they searched the barrel and found a few coarse grains stuck in a narrow groove inside the lid.
Maya had scrubbed the barrel every week, but the groove was too thin to see into.
During polish week, the hidden grit had fallen out and scratched the stones as they turned.
The school rock show was fifteen days away, so Maya and Ms. Ortiz compared two fixes.
Maya could start over with coarse grit, which would take four more weeks.
Or she could scrub the lid groove with an old toothbrush and repeat only the fine grit and polish weeks.
Ms. Ortiz said the scratches were shallow enough for fine grit to remove them.
Maya chose the second fix, because it would take two weeks and be ready in time.
Two weeks later, the agates came out bright and smooth, and the next day Maya set twelve of them on a black cloth at the rock show.

passages.title: The Concert Moves Inside
sentences: The Harbor Middle School band had practiced for six weeks for its spring concert.
The concert was planned for two o'clock on Saturday, at the bandstand in the harbor park.
Maya would play the flute, and Leo would play the drums.
On Saturday morning, a strong wind began to blow in from the sea.
Flags on the harbor flapped hard, and paper cups rolled across the park.
At the bandstand, the wind kept lifting the sheet music off the music stands.
Ms. Gray, the music teacher, gathered the band under the roof of the bandstand.
"The wind has changed our plan, so let's list what we could do," she said calmly.
The band could play outside and hold the music down with clothespins.
They could move the concert to the school gym, which was free all afternoon.
Or they could wait and play on the next Saturday.
Maya tried two clothespins on her stand, but the wind still bent the pages and turned them over.
Leo said that many families had already planned to come today.
So the band chose the gym.
Moving the concert caused a new problem, because the families would go to the harbor, not the school.
Sam drew a simple map from the bandstand to the gym, and Ms. Gray taped copies to the bandstand posts.
The school also sent a message to every family about the new place.
At two o'clock, almost every chair in the gym was full.
The band played all six songs, and not one page blew away.

passages.title: The Cracked Wheel
sentences: Every spring, the observatory on Lantern Peaks holds Mars Day, and the biggest event is the rover challenge.
Behind the observatory is the Mars yard, a field of red sand, gravel and rocks that looks like the surface of Mars.
Each rover must drive from the starting line to a flag and back, and the fastest rover that finishes wins.
Priya wanted her rover to be faster this year.
So she replaced its heavy rubber wheels with light plastic wheels that she had printed on the school's 3D printer.
An hour before the challenge, Priya and Sam took the rover for a practice run.
Halfway across the yard, it rolled over a strip of sharp gravel, and one plastic wheel cracked.
After that, the cracked wheel could not grip the ground, so the rover kept pulling to the left.
It drove in a slow circle and never reached the flag.
Priya carried the rover back to her table and took a long, slow breath.
"My plan has to change, but we still have an hour," she said.
Sam remembered reading that a real rover on Mars once got holes in its wheels from sharp rocks.
Its team on Earth kept driving it, but they planned routes that went around the sharpest rocks.
Priya could do the same thing: put on her one spare plastic wheel and steer around the gravel.
That plan was fast, but if a second wheel cracked, she would have no spare left.
Her other choice was to put the old rubber wheels back on.
They were heavy and would make the rover slower, but they had crossed sharp gravel many times without any damage.
Priya read the rules again, and they said that a rover that stops before the flag gets no score.
She decided that finishing was more important than being fast, so she chose the rubber wheels.
In the challenge, her rover rolled straight over the gravel, touched the flag and came back.
It finished in third place, and Priya wrote a new goal in her notebook: design a light wheel that is also strong.

passages.title: The Rained-Out Dig
sentences: Last summer, paleontologists from the Harbor Town Museum discovered the bones of a duck-billed dinosaur in Red Rock Quarry.
Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils, which are the remains or traces of living things from long ago, preserved in rock.
This kind of dinosaur ate plants and lived more than 66 million years ago.
The museum invited Ms. Ortiz's science club to help with the excavation, or careful digging, on the first Saturday in October.
Maya packed her own soft brush and a notebook for sketching every bone the club uncovered.
But heavy rain fell all Friday night and continued into Saturday morning.
When the club arrived, the lead paleontologist, Dr. Bell, was waiting for them at the museum instead of the quarry.
She explained that the rain had turned the clay in the quarry into deep, slippery mud.
In mud, diggers cannot tell where a bone ends and the surrounding rock begins, so they could easily damage a fossil by accident.
For that reason, her team never excavates in the quarry while the ground is wet.
Maya looked down at her brush and was quiet for a moment.
Then she asked Dr. Bell what the club could do instead.
Dr. Bell described two possible choices.
The club could go home and wait for a dry Saturday to dig.
Or they could spend the morning in the museum's preparation lab, where workers carefully clean bones that were collected last summer.
Ben worried that the lab would be boring, but Dr. Bell promised that the club would use real tools on real fossils.
After a short discussion, the club voted for the lab.
In the lab, each student used a small metal pick and a soft brush to remove rock from around a bone.
The work was slow, because one careless scrape could chip the fossil underneath.
Maya uncovered part of a tooth, and she sketched it in her notebook.
Two weeks later, on a dry, sunny Saturday, the club finally excavated in the quarry and found a rib bone.

steps.say: The question asks why. A "why" answer tells what made something happen.
First, I find the sentence where the tower falls.
Then I read the sentence just before it, to see what happened first.
Pixel's tail hit a table leg, and the table shook. A shaking table can make a tall tower fall.
So the tower fell because Pixel's tail hit the table and made it shake.
